passages.title: 写作时间与优先级
paragraphs: Harlan Coben believes that if you're a writer, you'll find the time; and that if you can't find the time, then writing isn't a priority and you're not a writer. For him writing is a {{1}} job—a job like any other. He has {{2}} it with plumbing. He points out that a plumber doesn't wake up and say that he can't work with pipes today. {{3}}, like most writers these days, you're holding down a job to pay the bills, it's not {{4}} to find the time to write. But it's not impossible. It requires determination and single-mindedness. {{5}} that best-selling authors began writing when they were doing other things to earn a living. And today, even writers who are fairly {{6}} often have to do other work to {{7}} their writing income. As Harlan Coben has suggested, it's a {{8}} of priorities and some things you really enjoy. To make writing a priority, you'll have to {{9}} some of your day-to-day activities and some things you really enjoy. Depending on your {{10}} and your lifestyle, that might mean spending less time watching television or listening to music, though some people can write {{11}} they listen to music. You might have to {{12}} the amount of exercise or sport you do. You'll have to make social media an {{13}} activity rather than a daily, time-consuming {{14}}. There'll probably have to be less socializing with your friends and less time with your family. It's a {{15}} learning curve, and it won't always make you popular. There's just one thing you should try to keep at least some time for {{16}} your writing—and that's reading. Any writer needs to read as much and as widely as they can; it's the one {{17}} supporter—something you can't do without. Time is finite. The older you get, the {{18}} it seems to go. We need to use it carefully and as {{19}} as we can. That means prioritizing our activities so that we spend most time on the things we really want to do. If you're a writer, that means — {{20}} — writing.

questions.context: For him writing is a {{1}} job—a job like any other.
questions.explanation: 后句把写作与修管道类比（管道工不会一早醒来说今天修不了管子），说明写作在 Coben 眼中是一份平常的工作。干扰项 difficult/pleasant 与「-a job like any other」不符；steady 无据

questions.context: He has {{2}} it with plumbing.
questions.qtype: 动词词义 + 固定搭配
questions.explanation: compare A with B（把 A 与 B 相比）。confuse A with B / combine A with B / confront sb with sth 均不合语境

questions.context: {{3}}, like most writers these days, you're holding down a job to pay the bills, it's not {{4}} to find the time to write.
questions.explanation: 从句「你像如今多数作家一样有份养家的工作」与主句「__不容易找到时间写作」构成条件关系。Though 让步、Once 时间、Unless 否定条件，均不成立

questions.explanation: 由 even（甚至） 表递进：即便相当知名的作家也常需做别的工作。well-advised（审慎的）/well-informed（见多识广的）/well-chosen（精选的）均不符

questions.context: As Harlan Coben has suggested, it's a {{8}} of priorities and some things you really enjoy.

questions.explanation: it's a question of priorities（这是个优先级问题）。cause/purpose/condition 不与 of priorities 构成此搭配

questions.context: To make writing a priority, you'll have to {{9}} some of your day-to-day activities and some things you really enjoy.

questions.context: Depending on your {{10}} and your lifestyle, that might mean spending less time watching television or listening to music, though some people can write {{11}} they listen to music.
questions.explanation: 与 lifestyle 并列，且后文 watching television、listening to music 均属兴趣爱好

questions.explanation: 破折号后 and that's reading（那就是阅读）：除写作之外还有一件应保留时间的事。in place of 取代、in charge of 负责、in response to 回应，均逻辑不通

questions.explanation: 破折号后 something you can't do without 直译同义复现 → 不可或缺的。innovative 创新的、invisible 看不见的、instant 即时的，属音/形近干扰

questions.explanation: 与 carefully 并列：尽可能审慎、高效地利用时间。peacefully/generously/gratefully 与「利用时间」不搭

questions.context: If you're a writer, that means — {{20}} — writing.
questions.explanation: 全文收尾的用法延续：prioritising … spend most time on the things we really want to do → 如果你写作家，那意味着「最重要的是写作」。at most 至多、in turn 依次、on average 平均

passages.title: 小企业增长团队
paragraphs: Here's a common scenario that any number of entrepreneurs face today: you're the CEO of a small business, and though you're making a nice {{1}}, you need to find a way to take it to the next level. What you need to do is {{2}} growth by establishing a growth team. A growth team is made up of members from different departments within your company and it harnesses the power of collaboration to focus {{3}} on finding ways to grow. Let's look at a real-world {{4}}. Prior to forming a growth team, the software company BitTorrent had 50 employees working in the {{5}} departments of engineering, marketing and product development. This brought them good results until 2012, when their growth plateaued. The {{6}} was that too many customers were using the basic, free version of their product. And {{7}} improvements to the premium, paid version, few people were making the upgrade. Things changed, {{8}}, when an innovative project-marketing manager (PMM) came aboard, {{9}} a growth team and sparked the kind of {{10}} perspective they needed. By looking at engineering issues from a marketing point of view, it became clear that the {{11}} of upgrades wasn't due to a quality issue. Most customers were simply unaware of the premium version and what it offered. Armed with this {{12}}, the marketing and engineering teams joined forces to raise awareness by prominently {{13}} the premium version to users of the free version. {{14}}, upgrades skyrocketed, and revenue increased by 92 percent. But in order for your growth team to succeed, it needs to have a strong leader. It needs someone who can {{15}} the interdisciplinary team and keep them on course for improvement. This leader will {{16}} the target area, set clear goals and establish a time frame for the {{17}} of these goals. The growth leader is also {{18}} for keeping the team focused on moving forward and steering the team clear of distractions. {{19}} attractive new ideas can be distracting, the team leader must recognize when these ideas don't {{20}} the current goal and need to be put on the back burner.

passages.title: 社交生活与社交健康
paragraphs: Your social life is defined as 'the activities you do with other people, for pleasure, when you are not working'. It's important to have a social life, but what's right for one person won't be right for another. Some of us feel energised by spending lots of time with others, {{1}} some of us may feel drained, even if it's doing something we enjoy. 'This is why finding a {{2}} in your social life is key. Spending too much time on your own, not {{3}} others, can make you feel lonely and {{4}}. Loneliness is known to impact on your mental health and {{5}} a low mood. Anyone can feel lonely at any time. This might be especially true if, {{6}}, you are working from home and you are {{7}} on the usual social conversations that happen in an office. Other life changes can {{8}} periods of loneliness too, such as retirement, changing jobs or becoming a parent. It's important to recognise these feelings of loneliness. There are ways to {{9}} a social life, but it can feel overwhelming {{10}}. It's a great idea to start by thinking about hobbies you enjoy. You can then find groups and activities related to those where you will be able to meet {{11}} people. There are groups aimed at new parents, at those who want to {{12}} a new sport for the first time, or networking events for those in the same profession to meet up and {{13}} ideas. On the other hand, it's {{14}} possible to have too much of a social life. If you feel like you're always doing something and there is never any {{15}} in your calendar for downtime, you could suffer social burnout or social {{16}}. We all have our own social limit and it's important to recognise when you're feeling like it's all too much. Low mood, low energy, irritability and trouble sleeping could all be {{17}} of poor social health. Make sure you {{18}} some time in your diary when you're {{19}} for socialising and use this time to relax, {{20}}, and recover.

passages.title: 为什么难以开口求助
paragraphs: There are many understandable reasons why you might find it difficult to ask for help when you need it. Psychologists have been interested in this {{1}} for decades, not least because people’s widespread {{2}} to ask for help has led to some high-profile failures. Asking for help takes {{3}}. It involves communicating a need on your part—there's something you can't do. {{4}}, you're broadcasting your own weaknesses which can be {{5}}. You might worry about coming across as incompetent. You might have {{6}} about losing control of whatever it is you're asking for help with. {{7}} someone starts to help, perhaps they’ll take over, or get credit for your earlier efforts. Yet another {{8}} that might be worried about is being a nuisance or {{9}} the person you go to for help. If you struggle with low self-esteem, you might find it especially difficult to {{10}} for help because you have the added worry of the other person {{11}} your request. You might see such refusals as implying something {{12}} about the status of your relationship with them. To {{13}} these difficulties, try to remind yourself that everyone needs help sometimes. Nobody knows everything and can do everything all by themselves. And while you might {{14}} coming across as incompetent, there’s actually research that shows that advice-seekers are {{15}} as more competent, not less. Perhaps most encouraging of all is a paper from 2022 by researchers at Stanford University that involved a mix of contrived help-seeking interactions and asking people to {{16}} times they’d sought help in the past. The findings showed that help-seekers generally underestimate how {{17}} other people will be to help and how good it’ll make the help-giver feel (for most people, having the chance to help someone is highly {{18}}). So, bear all this in mind the next time you need to ask for help {{19}}, take care over who you ask and when you ask them. And if someone can't help right now, avoid taking it personally. They might just be too {{20}}, or they might not feel confident about their ability to help.

questions.context: Psychologists have been interested in this {{1}} for decades, not least because people’s widespread {{2}} to ask for help has led to some high-profile failures.
questions.explanation: this question 回指首句「为什么需要帮助时难以开口求助」这一问题。干扰项：A illusion 幻觉 / B discussion 讨论 / C tradition 传统。

questions.context: Psychologists have been interested in this {{1}} for decades, not least because people’s widespread {{2}} to ask for help has led to some high-profile failures.

questions.explanation: 与 being a nuisance（成为累赘）并列，语义一致 → 给求助对象带来不便。干扰项：A overpraising 过度表扬 / B outperforming 胜过 / C reassessing 重新评估。

questions.context: If you struggle with low self-esteem, you might find it especially difficult to {{10}} for help because you have the added worry of the other person {{11}} your request.
questions.qtype: 动词短语辨析 + 固定搭配
questions.explanation: reach out for help 为固定搭配「寻求帮助」。干扰项：B settle down 安顿 / C turn over 移交 / D look back 回顾。

questions.context: If you struggle with low self-esteem, you might find it especially difficult to {{10}} for help because you have the added worry of the other person {{11}} your request.
questions.qtype: 动词词义辨析 + 下文复现
questions.explanation: 后句 you might see such refusals（把这种拒绝看作…）中 refusals 直接复现 → 拒绝你的请求。干扰项：B considering / C criticising / D evaluating。

questions.context: You might see such refusals as implying something {{12}} about the status of your relationship with them.
questions.explanation: 「把拒绝视为暗示你们关系状态中负面的东西」，与 self-esteem 低者的心理一致。干扰项：A unnecessary / C strange / D impractical。

questions.context: To {{13}} these difficulties, try to remind yourself that everyone needs help sometimes.
questions.explanation: 后文「提醒自己人人都需要帮助」是克服上述困难的方法。overcome difficulties 搭配。干扰项：A explain / B identify / C predict。

questions.context: And while you might {{14}} coming across as incompetent, there’s actually research that shows that advice-seekers are {{15}} as more competent, not less.
questions.explanation: 与前句 exposing weakness 呼应：「你可能害怕显得无能」，fear doing 搭配。干扰项：A deny 否认 / B forget / C miss。

questions.context: And while you might {{14}} coming across as incompetent, there’s actually research that shows that advice-seekers are {{15}} as more competent, not less.
questions.qtype: 动词词义辨析（被动语态）
questions.explanation: be perceived as = 被认为。「寻求建议者被认为更有能力，而非更差」。干扰项：A disguised 伪装 / C followed / D introduced。

questions.context: Perhaps most encouraging of all is a paper from 2022 by researchers at Stanford University that involved a mix of contrived help-seeking interactions and asking people to {{16}} times they’d sought help in the past.
questions.explanation: 「让人们回忆过去求助过的时刻」。干扰项：B classify 分类 / C analyse 分析 / D compare 比较。

questions.context: The findings showed that help-seekers generally underestimate how {{17}} other people will be to help and how good it’ll make the help-giver feel (for most people, having the chance to help someone is highly {{18}}).
questions.explanation: 「求助者低估了他人乐于帮忙的程度」，be willing to help。干扰项：A brave / B disapproving 不赞成的 / D hesitant 犹豫的。

questions.context: The findings showed that help-seekers generally underestimate how {{17}} other people will be to help and how good it’ll make the help-giver feel (for most people, having the chance to help someone is highly {{18}}).
questions.explanation: 「对多数人而言，有机会帮助别人是很有回报感的」，与 how good it'll make the help-giver feel 呼应。干扰项：A relaxing / B surprising / D demanding 费力的。

questions.context: So, bear all this in mind the next time you need to ask for help {{19}}, take care over who you ask and when you ask them.
questions.explanation: 前句 bear all this in mind，后句 take care over… 为递进补充建议。干扰项：A Thus 因此（因果）/ C Finally 最后 / D Instead 相反。

questions.context: They might just be too {{20}}, or they might not feel confident about their ability to help.
questions.qtype: 形容词词义辨析 + 常识
questions.explanation: 「他们可能只是太忙了」——解释为何不能帮忙的客观中性原因，与 don't take it personally 一致。干扰项：A polite / B proud / D lazy（贬义，与劝慰语气冲突）。

passages.title: 自尊与两种心理防御
paragraphs: Most of us strive for self-respect — to see ourselves in a positive light, to be {{1}} of who we are. Any comments or experiences that undermine those feelings of self-worth can be uncomfortable and it's only {{2}} to want to avoid them. But the thing is, {{3}} your self-worth really is being undermined is, to a large degree, subjective. Much of it comes down to your {{4}} of what someone said or did. When you take things personally, you're interpreting these situations as saying something significant and negative about you as a person. Say your boss picks holes in your sales report, and you come away feeling like this means she thinks you're a {{5}} member of staff. Or, two of your friends cancel your {{6}} get-together at the pub and you interpret this as meaning they're bored of you. Psychologists have a {{7}} for this way of thinking: personalisation. But the {{8}} is that your boss might view you very highly. It's just you made some {{9}} in the report and she wanted to point these out so that you do better next time. {{10}}, in the case of your friends cancelling, perhaps they both felt unwell that weekend or they just {{11}} their minds. In both {{12}} —and others that we all experience— there’s another {{13}} at work that psychologists call mind reading. This is when you assume to know what other people are thinking about you, when you can't really know without {{14}} them directly. One simple way to avoid {{15}} personalisation and mind reading is to challenge your negative assumptions of what's {{16}}. When you find yourself taking a situation personally, try to think of other interpretations that are less focused on you — especially in the sense of saying anything deep or {{17}} about you. When you do this, it might help to try to put yourself in other people’s shoes. The fact your boss took the time to give you {{18}} at all means they care enough to want to help you {{19}}. When it comes to your friends — maybe it's because your friendship is so {{20}} that they felt able to cancel at late notice.

questions.context: Most of us strive for self-respect — to see ourselves in a positive light, to be {{1}} of who we are.
questions.qtype: 形容词词义辨析 + 同义解释
questions.explanation: 破折号后两个并列不定式是对 strive for self-respect 的具体阐释：to see ourselves in a positive light（积极看待自己）与 to be __ of who we are 同向并列 → 需正向情感词。且 be proud of 为固定搭配。干扰项：A afraid（与 positive 矛盾）/ B critical / D tolerant。

questions.context: Any comments or experiences that undermine those feelings of self-worth can be uncomfortable and it's only {{2}} to want to avoid them.
questions.qtype: 形容词词义辨析 + 顺承逻辑
questions.explanation: 前句「任何削弱自我价值感的评论或经历都会令人不适」，and 顺承 → 「想要回避它们是很自然的」。it's only natural to do 为常用句式。干扰项：A risky / C admirable（程度过重）/ D foolish（方向相反）。

questions.context: But the thing is, {{3}} your self-worth really is being undermined is, to a large degree, subjective.
questions.explanation: __ your self-worth really is being undermined 是整个句子的主语，谓语是 is subjective。「自尊是否真的受损」这一"待判断之事"是主观的 → whether。干扰项：B where / C why / D how 均无法与 is subjective 合理衔接。

questions.context: Much of it comes down to your {{4}} of what someone said or did.
questions.qtype: 名词词义辨析 + 复现呼应
questions.explanation: 前句落脚于 subjective（主观），本句解释主观性体现在哪一环 → 「很大程度上取决于你对别人言行的感知/理解」。干扰项：A citation 引用 / B imitation 模仿 / D introduction 介绍，均与"主观理解"无关。

questions.context: Say your boss picks holes in your sales report, and you come away feeling like this means she thinks you're a {{5}} member of staff.
questions.qtype: 形容词词义辨析 + 例证逻辑
questions.explanation: 举例说明"个人化"：老板挑你销售报告的毛病 → 你解读成「她认为你是个差劲的员工」。由"对事"错误推及"对人"。干扰项：B loyal / C creative（与"挑毛病"矛盾）/ D shy（与工作能力无关）。

questions.context: Or, two of your friends cancel your {{6}} get-together at the pub and you interpret this as meaning they're bored of you.
questions.qtype: 形容词/过去分词作定语
questions.explanation: 「两个朋友取消了你们在酒吧的计划好的聚会」，planned get-together 符合生活逻辑，且与 cancel 自然搭配。干扰项：A sponsored 赞助的 / B crowded 拥挤的 / C disputed 有争议的。

questions.context: Psychologists have a {{7}} for this way of thinking: personalisation.
questions.qtype: 固定搭配 + 下文复现
questions.explanation: Psychologists have a term for this way of thinking: personalisation. — 冒号后即该术语。have a term for sth. = 对某事有专门称呼。干扰项：A method / C design / D goal。

questions.context: But the {{8}} is that your boss might view you very highly.
questions.qtype: 名词词义辨析 + 转折逻辑
questions.explanation: But 转折，由主观臆测转向客观事实：「但现实可能是老板其实很看重你」，the reality is that… 为固定表达。干扰项：A evidence / B theory / C condition。

questions.context: It's just you made some {{9}} in the report and she wanted to point these out so that you do better next time.
questions.qtype: 名词词义辨析 + 因果
questions.explanation: 「你只是在报告里犯了些错误，她指出来是希望你下次做得更好」，made some mistakes 与 picks holes in your sales report 呼应。干扰项：A complaints / B choices / D suggestions。

questions.context: {{10}}, in the case of your friends cancelling, perhaps they both felt unwell that weekend or they just {{11}} their minds.
questions.explanation: 本段并列分析两个例子（老板批评报告 / 朋友取消聚会），二者同向类比——主观解读都可能偏离事实 → 「同样地」。干扰项：B Relatively / C Accordingly（因果，不成立）/ D Contrarily（对立，与同向类比矛盾）。

questions.context: {{10}}, in the case of your friends cancelling, perhaps they both felt unwell that weekend or they just {{11}} their minds.
questions.qtype: 动词词义辨析 + 固定搭配
questions.explanation: they just changed their minds（他们只是改变了主意），与 or 前的 felt unwell 并列，同为爽约的中性解释。干扰项：A opened / C trained / D cleared，均不与 minds 构成合理搭配。

questions.context: In both {{12}} —and others that we all experience— there’s another {{13}} at work that psychologists call mind reading.
questions.qtype: 名词词义辨析 + 指代上文
questions.explanation: 「在这两个例子中——以及我们都经历过的其他例子中——」回指上文两则案例。干扰项：A quotations 引文 / B experiments 实验 / C questions 问题。

questions.context: In both {{12}} —and others that we all experience— there’s another {{13}} at work that psychologists call mind reading.
questions.explanation: 「还有另一种在起作用的心理过程，心理学家称之为 mindreading」，at work（在起作用）修饰 process。干扰项：B objective 目标 / C outcome 结果 / D background 背景。

questions.context: This is when you assume to know what other people are thinking about you, when you can't really know without {{14}} them directly.
questions.qtype: 动词词义辨析 + 语义呼应
questions.explanation: 「你自以为知道别人在想什么，可实际上除非直接问他们，你根本无从知晓」——这正是"读心术"的要害。干扰项：A blaming / B warning / C teaching。

questions.context: One simple way to avoid {{15}} personalisation and mind reading is to challenge your negative assumptions of what's {{16}}.
questions.explanation: 「避免陷入个人化与读心术的一个简单方法」，engage in（从事、陷入）与 personalisation / mindreading 搭配。干扰项：A arguing about 争论 / B accounting for 解释 / D interfering with 干扰。

questions.context: One simple way to avoid {{15}} personalisation and mind reading is to challenge your negative assumptions of what's {{16}}.
questions.qtype: 动词词义辨析 + 逻辑
questions.explanation: 「挑战你对已经发生之事的负面假设」——事实必然是已发生的。干扰项：B continued / C returned / D disappeared。

questions.context: When you find yourself taking a situation personally, try to think of other interpretations that are less focused on you — especially in the sense of saying anything deep or {{17}} about you.
questions.qtype: 形容词词义辨析 + 并列结构
questions.explanation: deep or __ about you 由 or 连接，语义须与 deep（深层的）高度一致 → 根本性的。干扰项：A casual 随意的 / B obvious / C familiar。

questions.context: The fact your boss took the time to give you {{18}} at all means they care enough to want to help you {{19}}.
questions.qtype: 名词词义辨析 + 上文呼应
questions.explanation: 「老板愿意花时间给你反馈本身就说明她在乎你」，与第 9 题 point these out so that you do better next time 呼应。干扰项：A reward 奖励 / C trust 信任 / D proof 证明。

questions.context: The fact your boss took the time to give you {{18}} at all means they care enough to want to help you {{19}}.
questions.explanation: 「……说明她在乎你、想帮你进步」，help you improve。干扰项：A innovate 创新 / B concentrate 专注 / D relax 放松。

questions.context: When it comes to your friends — maybe it's because your friendship is so {{20}} that they felt able to cancel at late notice.
questions.qtype: 形容词词义辨析 + 反常识推理
questions.explanation: 「也许正因为你们的友谊如此牢固，他们才敢临时爽约」——用反向推理消解"他们厌倦你了"的负面解读。干扰项：A strange / C vulnerable 脆弱的（逻辑相反）/ D valuable（多修饰事物）。
